summary: Jake Goldsmith argues that people and experts alike are pressured to speak authoritatively before accumulating real knowledge, which erodes trust in expertise and threatens democracy. He contends that experts who speak outside their narrow domains obscure their genuine expertise and make themselves appear less trustworthy. He also criticizes applying generalized political rules across nations without local history, and concludes that truth requires prudence and responsibility. The piece credits philosopher Vlad Vexler and the late Bernard Williams as influences.
one_line: Jake Goldsmith argues that experts speaking beyond their narrow domains erode public trust and threaten democracy, drawing on Bernard Williams.
key_facts: Jake Goldsmith credits the philosopher Vlad Vexler, whom he recommends as a sound analyst of political philosophy, and the late Bernard Williams for his thinking.
The note argues that people are pressured to 'generate knowledge' by talking and self-styling long before real accumulation of knowledge and reflection occurs.

The note states that the implications of people expressing themselves before accumulating knowledge are anti-democratic, including further democratic degradation, despotism, more conflict and violence.
The note says experts are pressured to speak grandly on things they know little or nothing about.
The note states that academic experts are commonly invited to speak about anything, though their knowledge is limited to a specific area and they are not omniscient.
The note argues that when experts talk outside their realm of competence and do so poorly, they obscure what they are genuinely knowledgeable about.
The note states that 'Expertise matters. Without it we have a crisis of trust and a real threat to democracy.'
Speaking with Bernard Williams, the note says democracy is bound to the practical virtue of truthfulness and to trustworthy institutions.
The note argues that experts who talk about anything and everything, when their expertise is deep but narrow, make themselves appear less trustworthy.
The note criticizes applying generalised rules of politics to nations, using the USA or Russia as examples, instead of investigating local developments and history.
The note cites Democritus: 'truth, as Democritus once said, is in the depths.'
The note concludes that truth requires prudence and responsibility, both in short supply across the world.
Jake Goldsmith, 25, is a writer with cystic fibrosis and founder of The Barbellion Prize, a book prize for ill and disabled authors.
Jake Goldsmith is the author of a memoir titled Neither Weak Nor Obtuse.
